transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 08:42 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Maria Lopez (HealthBridge Dir Eng), Samir Patel (CTO), Jenna Cho (DevOps), Evan Ortiz (Security)

Summary: Quick demo and walkthrough of how Redwood handles rate limits, quotas, and multi-tenant controls using org/project keys. Conversation covered tradeoffs between hosted and dedicated, audit logs, and how bursting works.

00:00 Alex Carter: hey everyone thanks for joining, i think we've got about 40 minutes, we'll run through the console and then demo keys and quotas, priya will jump into the technical bits
00:12 Maria Lopez: thanks alex, yeah we wanted to focus on how we can limit per-tenant usage and make sure noisy customers dont blow up our cost or latency
00:20 Priya Singh: cool, we'll start with the high-level map — Redwood supports org-level policies and project-level keys. so you can set organization-wide default quotas and then override per project.
00:35 Samir Patel: is that the same as the api key scoping? like can i create keys with granular permissions and rate limits per key?
00:42 Priya Singh: yep, keys are scoping objects associated with projects. you can attach a rate limit policy (tokens per minute/hour), and also a quota cap, so if a single key exceeds quota it gets blocked or throttled depending on the policy
00:58 Jenna Cho: whats the behavior on bursts? we have planed big bursts for certain events — like 2k qps for a minute — will they be dropped or queued?
01:10 Priya Singh: good q. we use a leaky-bucket / token-bucket hybrid — short bursts are absorbed up to a burst_capacity. there are two knobs: steady_rate and burst_capacity. if the burst is above burst_capacity then requests are throttled and will receive 429s. you can configure burst windows per project or fall back to org default.
01:30 Evan Ortiz: from a security point, are those rate limit events logged? we need audit trails for throttling events and per-tenant usage for SOC2 audits
01:40 Alex Carter: yes, all limit events (throttled, quota-exceeded) are recorded in the audit log with the key id, project, and request metadata. priya will show where in the console
01:50 Priya Singh: jumping into the console — so here's the Projects page, you can see Project: portal-api, billing-api etc. clicking into a project shows keys, policies, and usage charts (you should see them in the screenshot we shared)
02:05 Priya Singh: (demo) creating a project key: give it a name, scope (read/write), attach policy. you can pick a predefined policy like 'default dev policy' or create custom one — custom lets you specify rate limit (rps, rpm), token limits (tokens/min) and hard quota monthly tokens
02:30 Maria Lopez: will that integration work with our current API gateway? we have kong in front of our services and we do some per-tenant sharding there
02:40 Priya Singh: yes you can use Redwood keys directly in your app or relay via your gateway. keys are stateless tokens — Redwood validates them on ingress. if you proxy through kong, you'd forward the same key header. policies are enforced at the Redwood edge or at Dedicated node depending on deployment
03:00 Samir Patel: talk through Dedicated vs Hosted here specifically for quotas and rate limits — we've been leaning towards Dedicated because we need predictable p99 latency and throughput for peak windows
03:12 Alex Carter: high level: hosted gives you per-tenant controls and quotas but it's subject to multi-tenant resource pooling, so for hard throughput guarantees we recommend Dedicated + reserved capacity. Dedicated runs your projects on reserved GPU pools and enforces quotas at the per-node ingress — you'll get SLA-backed latency targets
03:30 Samir Patel: does Dedicated still give you org/project keys or do we lose some multi-tenant controls when we move on-prem?
03:38 Priya Singh: Dedicated preserves the same control plane and key semantics. the difference is the serving plane runs on your reserved GPUs (or in your VPC for private deployments). policies in the control plane still manage keys and quotas; enforcement happens locally on the Dedicated nodes
03:55 Jenna Cho: ok, can we set per-customer cost accounting? like tags or labels so we can break down token spend per tenant in billing exports
04:05 Alex Carter: yes we have per-key/ per-project tagging and a cost-export CSV you can ingest. Redwood Console has a token-level cost breakdown and you can export per-project and per-key usage for chargebacks
04:20 Maria Lopez: that will help. our primary concern is noisy tenants causing cost spikes. can we set throttles that escalate — maybe soft throttle first, then hard block?
04:30 Priya Singh: absolutely; you can make a policy with an action chain: first soft_throttle (slows responses / queue), then on continued violation escalate to hard_block or route to a cheaper model. we also support fallbacks — for example route overflow traffic to a cheaper quantized model to preserve availability
04:50 Samir Patel: interesting — how do fallbacks affect chat state and kv cache? will users notice context loss?
05:00 Priya Singh: fallbacks are model-level and we try to preserve KV cache by storing prefix caches — there can be slight differences due to model variance but the runtime stitches KV caches and attempts to maintain conversation continuity. we always recommend testing with your prompt sets
05:20 Alex Carter: (interruption) just to add — Optimize will surface recommendations like which projects to co-locate on Dedicated and batching configs to reduce unit cost while preserving latency
05:30 Maria Lopez: can Optimize suggest per-project quantization profiles? we have compliance teams who worry about quality regressions
05:38 Priya Singh: yes, Optimize suggests quant and model family recommendations by workload. it runs evals on your prompt sets and flags regressions; you can tie alerts to a prompt suite so if quality drops after a config change you get notified
05:55 Jenna Cho: show us an example policy in the UI please
06:00 Priya Singh: sure — opening policy editor: here is an org default: 100k tokens/day and burst of 3k tokens/min. then project override: 'portal-api' has 10k tokens/min steady with 5k burst. you can also set per-key caps — great for service accounts vs end-user keys
06:25 Maria Lopez: how granular are the logs? request-level? token-level?
06:30 Priya Singh: logs are at request-level with metadata (key id, project, model, tokens_in/out, latency). usage aggregates are precomputed for charts. audit trails include policy-change events with user and timestamp
06:45 Evan Ortiz: where does the audit log live for private deployments? we need control over retention and export to our SIEM
06:52 Priya Singh: for Private deployments you can keep audit logs on your S3/kinesis or push them to your SIEM. the control plane supports forwarding and you can set retention via config. for Dedicated we keep logs for the SLA-defined window but you can request longer export retention
07:10 Samir Patel: ok on the enforcement side, what's the observable signal when a project hits quota — is there an alert? can we hook it into our paging?
07:20 Priya Singh: yes you can set alerting thresholds by project or key (e.g., 80% of quota) and hook them to webhook or PagerDuty. Console also shows real-time quota meters and a throttling activity feed
07:35 Maria Lopez: i'd like to demo the api behavior — what header do we send and what responses look like on throttles
07:42 Priya Singh: header is Authorization: Bearer <project_key>. on a normal overage you'll get 429 with body {"error":"quota_exceeded","retry_after":30} and response headers X-Redwood-Quota-Remaining, X-Redwood-Quota-Limit.
07:58 Jenna Cho: is the error body standardized across hosted / dedicated? some of our gateway logic depends on consistent codes
08:05 Priya Singh: yes codes and headers are consistent across deployment modes. if you're using custom proxies we recommend normalizing the headers in the gateway so downstream services behave the same
08:18 Alex Carter: (to Maria) do you have a timeline in mind for pilot and what success looks like?
08:25 Maria Lopez: we want to run a 3-month pilot targeting two high-traffic endpoints. success criteria: under 100ms p95 for portal-api, predictable cost under our budget, and no data exfiltration risk. security needs SOC2 docs and log export working
08:40 Alex Carter: got it. we'll send a pilot playbook and trial org keys. priya will run a benchmark with your sample traces
08:48 Priya Singh: i'll need the request distribution and worst-case payload sizes. jenna, could you share those?
08:55 Jenna Cho: yes i'll put together a small CSV with percentiles and endpoints by friday
09:00 Samir Patel: one more Q on multi-tenant controls — can we auto-rotate keys and revoke per-project without downtime?
09:08 Priya Singh: yes rotation is supported. you can create a new key and flip in your gateway; Redwood supports key grace windows where old keys are accepted for N minutes. revocation is immediate if you choose hard revoke
09:20 Maria Lopez: any limitations on number of projects or keys? we have hundreds of tenants and want a key per-tenant
09:28 Priya Singh: no hard limit — Console handles thousands of projects and keys. for very large fleets we recommend API-driven key provisioning using our management APIs and tagging conventions
09:40 Evan Ortiz: about encryption — do keys ever land in logs? we need to ensure PII and keys aren't exposed
09:45 Priya Singh: we mask keys in UI and logs by default and only store hashed forms in the control plane. request logs have key id, not raw token. you can also enforce logging redaction rules on export
09:58 Alex Carter: ok wrapping up, next steps and recap
10:02 Alex Carter: will send SOC2 and network diagram, provide trial org and project keys, priya will prepare benchmark plan and run next tuesday if we get traces, jenna will share traces by friday
10:15 Maria Lopez: thanks all, this was helpful — we'll review the security docs and sync on internal stakeholders
10:25 Priya Singh: thank you. feel free to reach out if you want deeper perf deep dive or private deployment pricing

Transcript notes: occasional transcription artifacts — speaker labels may be slightly off at times. references to console screens / screenshots were made (we shared deck and links in chat).
